Respiratory Infection in a Child

green mucus is not a bacterial sign · one side is a foreign body · typical vs atypical pneumoniaWhich side, how long and how sick, and does the illness span the upper and lower airway?

1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Read the side and the days before the color: pus alone is not bacterial; one foul side in a well toddler nasal foreign body; bilateral sinusitis must pass one of the Bacterial sinusitisSymptoms for 10 days or more without improvement; fever of 39 °C or more with severe symptoms for 3 to 4 days; or worsening after a cold had begun to improve ("double sickening")
  • Sore throat in a child: test before treating; penicillin prevents rheumatic fever, not poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
  • Pneumonia: abrupt, febrile, productive and lobar pneumococcus, amoxicillin; gradual dry cough at school age with a film worse than the child Mycoplasma, a macrolide
What it is

Nasal discharge, sore throat, ear pain or cough with fever in a child

Sort by

one side or both how many days how sick upper airway or chest

Hands off

Allergic rhinitis: ; orbital and other complications: ; rheumatic fever: ; cold agglutinin hemolysis: ; subacute cough with a known contact:

2Urgent risks
MucormycosisBlack or white turbinates or palate in ketoacidosis, neutropenia or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection with a CD4 (helper T-cell) count under 50

If the nasal tissue is necrotic, choose surgical debridement with amphotericin B.

Button batteryA button battery or paired magnets in the nose

If one is seen, choose emergency removal before the septum perforates.

3Differential
Causes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Acute bacterial sinusitisBilateral pus, often with fever and cough, after a coldPasses a door; amoxicillin-clavulanate, no imaging
Nasal foreign bodyOne side, foul, purulent, at times bloody; well, afebrile, 1 to 6 years; the insertion usually unseenOther side normal; remove it: blow with the other side shut, then instruments Nasal foreign bodyWith the open nostril held closed, a parent covers the child’s mouth with theirs and blows once; left in place, it brings sinusitis, periorbital cellulitis or aspiration.
Viral upper respiratory infection (URI)Afebrile, well, a few days of runny nose and coughClear eardrums, no exudate, clear lungs; supportive care
Adenoid hypertrophyMouth breathing, snoring, nasal voiceChronic bilateral obstruction
Strep pharyngitisFever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, no coughPositive rapid test or culture; penicillin or amoxicillin
Acute otitis mediaBulging, red eardrumReduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; high-dose amoxicillin
Typical pneumonia (S. pneumoniae)Abrupt high fever, productive cough, chest pain; looks illOne lobe consolidated; amoxicillin Pneumonia1 to 3 months: Chlamydia trachomatis, afebrile, with a staccato cough and eosinophilia. Under 5: mostly viruses, led by respiratory syncytial virus, then adenovirus, parainfluenza and human metapneumovirus. From 5: S. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila.
Atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma pneumoniae)Gradual over 1 to 2 weeks, dry cough, low fever, still active; school ageBilateral diffuse film, worse than the child; macrolide Atypical pneumoniaDoxycycline is an alternative; short courses are now accepted under 8 years. ComplicationsNo cell wall, so Gram stain misses it and penicillin does not work. Cold agglutinin (IgM) hemolysis; erythema multiforme, its second infectious cause after herpes simplex virus; Guillain-Barré syndrome. Older patientsWater systems, hotels or cruise ships, diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia: Legionella, urine antigen. Birds: Chlamydophila psittaci. Farm animals: Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), later hepatitis or culture-negative endocarditis. Hoarseness in a young adult: Chlamydophila pneumoniae.
Viral pneumoniaUnder 5; bilateral crackles, with or without wheezeMost often a virus at this age: RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) and others
Allergic rhinitisSneezing and itch; clear discharge on both sides; smoke and pets raise the riskPale, boggy turbinates; intranasal corticosteroid
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Anemia or dark urine during a Mycoplasma pneumoniaCold agglutinin (IgM) hemolysisSupports Mycoplasma
Otitis no better after 2 to 3 days of amoxicillin, or back within 30 daysResistant otitisAmoxicillin-clavulanate
Febrile child with no heart disease and a perihilar infiltratePneumonia, not heart failureHeart failure in children follows congenital heart disease or malnutrition
Smoking parent, pet dogAllergic rhinitis riskAllergy is bilateral and clear, never one foul side
HIV infection with a CD4 count well over 50, red swollen turbinatesNot mucormycosisThat needs white or black tissue

Pause point. The bait: green discharge or a single high fever read as bacterial sinusitis. Count the days and check the side; and a child who looks better than the film is Mycoplasma, not pneumococcus.

Practice
  1. 3-year-old boy has had 2 days of green nasal discharge playful and eating well tympanic membranes clear and mobile on pneumatic otoscopy no pharyngeal exudate; lungs clear Discharge from both nostrils Afebrile · HR 110/min · oxygen saturation 99% → Viral upper respiratory infection → the green comes from neutrophil myeloperoxidase in any inflammation, so 2 days of colored discharge in a well, afebrile child is viral: supportive care. Sinusitis must pass a door (10 days, 3 to 4 consecutive days or more of high fever with purulence, or double worsening); otitis media needs a bulging, immobile membrane
  2. 6-year-old boy has a sudden onset of high fever with shaking chills cough productive of rust-colored sputum chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation Ill appearing; right-sided chest pain T 39.8°C · HR 140/min → Streptococcus pneumoniae → abrupt onset, rigors, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation and an ill appearance separate pneumococcus from Mycoplasma, which is gradual and diffuse; Legionella brings diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia in an older smoker
  3. 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of foul-smelling, purulent discharge from the left naris only white bead visible just inside the left naris right naris normal Active, eating well, calm and cooperative; no cough Afebrile → Positive-pressure expulsion → a visible bead in a calm child comes out first with positive pressure (the parent's kiss, or blowing with the other naris closed); instruments if it fails, ENT endoscopy if not visible. No imaging, since most objects are radiolucent, and antibiotics leave the object in place
  4. 9-year-old girl is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia now jaundiced and pale hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positive for C3 Fingers turn white in the cold T 37.9°C · HR 118/min → Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia → Mycoplasma triggers IgM against the I antigen: a Coombs-positive cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia, sometimes with Raynaud. Fingers that blanch in the cold and a C3-positive direct antiglobulin test pick the cold type over warm autoimmune hemolysis or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
  5. 4-year-old girl has had 2 days of runny nose with green discharge her mother asks whether the green color means she needs an antibiotic Playful; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · lungs clear → No; neutrophils color it in any inflammation → the green is myeloperoxidase in neutrophils recruited by any inflammation, viral included, so color never proves bacteria; duration, fever and double worsening decide
  6. 35-year-old woman who breeds parrots at home has 1 week of dry cough and fever severe headache spleen tip palpable chest x-ray: patchy infiltrate, no hilar adenopathy No farm animal contact; no travel T 39.0°C · HR 96/min → Chlamydophila psittaci → a pet parrot with severe headache and splenomegaly is psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci). Histoplasma comes from soil rich in bird or bat droppings and typically enlarges the hilar or mediastinal nodes, which this film lacks; Coxiella needs farm animals, sheep or parturient cats
  7. 3-year-old boy has had 12 days of nasal discharge without improvement thick purulent discharge from both nostrils daytime cough No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.1°C · HR 112/min · tympanic membranes mobile → Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → 10 days or more without improvement is the first door to acute bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate, with no imaging. The persistence, not the color, is what separates it from a viral cold; allergy gives clear discharge with sneezing and itch
  8. 10-year-old boy has had 2 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough no improvement after 4 days of amoxicillin bilateral crackles; diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray Walking around and attending school T 37.9°C · white blood cell count 7,800/mm³ → Mycoplasma has no cell wall → a gradual, diffuse picture in a school-aged child is Mycoplasma, which has no cell wall, so beta-lactams cannot work: switch to a macrolide. Resistant H. influenzae or pneumococcus would still be a typical, focal pneumonia
  9. 3-year-old boy has clear rhinorrhea and frequent sneezing itchy, watery eyes seasonal recurrence each spring for 2 years pale, boggy nasal turbinates Father smokes; a cat at home Afebrile · HR 100/min → Allergic rhinitis → bilateral clear discharge, itch and pale, boggy turbinates are allergic rhinitis, and smoke and pets raise its risk: an intranasal corticosteroid. Sinusitis is purulent and must pass a door; the itch and the seasonal pattern point to allergy over a vasomotor cause
  10. 2-year-old girl pushed something from the television remote into her nose 2 hours ago her brother saw it now right-sided nosebleed and dark discharge smooth, gray, coin-shaped object deep in the right naris Afebrile · breathing comfortably · oxygen saturation 99% → Immediate removal in the emergency department → a coin-shaped object from a remote is a button battery: pressure and current necrose the mucosa and can perforate the septum, and a nosebleed or dark discharge is the tell, so remove it now. An outpatient endoscopy or an antibiotic recheck lets the injury progress
  11. 2-year-old boy has 3 days of cough, runny nose and wheeze diffuse wheezes and crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial pattern, no consolidation Attends daycare T 38.3°C · respiratory rate 44/min · oxygen saturation 95% → Viral pneumonia → under 5, viruses lead: RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus. Mycoplasma belongs to age 5 and older, and lobar bacterial pneumonia gives a focal consolidation
  12. 5-year-old girl had an upper respiratory illness that improved over 5 days on day 8, new fever worsening purulent nasal discharge Tympanic membranes mobile; lungs clear; eating less T 39.5°C · HR 124/min → Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate → an illness that improves and then worsens with new fever is double worsening: acute bacterial sinusitis, treated with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Supportive care alone ignores a door already crossed; the diagnosis is clinical, so no sinus computed tomography (CT)
  13. 28-year-old woman who works on a sheep farm has 10 days of fever and dry cough helped with lambing and a cat's delivery last month No rash, joint pain or bird contact T 39.2°C · alanine aminotransferase 140 U/L → Coxiella burnetii → farm animals, sheep and parturient cats with hepatitis and no rash are Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), which can cause culture-negative endocarditis later. Brucella also spreads to people in contact with livestock, but it brings cyclical fever with migratory arthralgia or sacroiliitis, often from unpasteurized dairy; psittacosis needs bird exposure, which she denies
  14. 3-year-old boy: 2 weeks of nasal discharge, first clear, now thick, foul right naris: pus, red swollen mucosa and turbinates; left normal Human immunodeficiency virus since birth, treated; CD4 520/mm³ Father smokes; pet dog Afebrile · playful · no cough → Nasal foreign body → one-sided foul pus in a well, afebrile toddler is a nasal foreign body: remove it with positive pressure or instruments. Sinusitis is bilateral and usually brings fever and cough; the smoking father and the pet dog raise allergy risk, but allergy is bilateral and clear; human immunodeficiency virus invites mucormycosis, but a CD4 count of 520 and red, not white or black, turbinates leave mucormycosis out. Afebrile, playful and without cough, he has no systemic signs
  15. 11-year-old girl had a dry cough and low-grade fever 3 weeks ago weakness rising from feet to thighs over 4 days absent ankle and knee reflexes sensation normal, no sensory level Pupils and bladder function normal HR 98/min → Guillain-Barré syndrome → ascending weakness weeks after a respiratory illness is a postinfectious complication: Guillain-Barré syndrome. Mycoplasma can also cause encephalitis and transverse myelitis, but normal sensation with no sensory level and normal bladder function argue against a cord lesion, and normal pupils argue against botulism
  16. 7-year-old boy has had 3 days of runny nose and cough mild maxillary pain profuse yellow-green nasal discharge tender upper cheeks Well appearing; no fever for the past 48 hours T 37.2°C · HR 96/min → Saline irrigation and analgesics → 3 days of symptoms, afebrile for 48 hours, meets no door, so this is viral rhinosinusitis despite the colored discharge: supportive care with saline irrigation and analgesics. Amoxicillin-clavulanate waits for a door; an antihistamine treats allergy, which gives clear discharge with itch
  17. 8-year-old boy is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia target lesions on the hands and feet painful oral mucositis with crusted lips raised three-ring targets; no skin sloughing Cough improving over the past week T 38.2°C · HR 110/min → Erythema multiforme / MIRM → target lesions with mucositis during Mycoplasma infection are erythema multiforme or MIRM (Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis); Mycoplasma is the leading infectious cause of erythema multiforme after herpes simplex virus. Raised, typical targets with three rings and no epidermal detachment pick erythema multiforme over Stevens-Johnson syndrome, whose target-like lesions are atypical, with two zones. The Mycoplasma link to targets and mucositis is what this stem shows; nothing in it builds a Kawasaki picture
  18. 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of a viral upper respiratory illness green nasal discharge from both nostrils improving each day Eating and sleeping normally; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · HR 104/min → Prescribe antibiotics → an improving viral illness meets no door; antibiotics do not shorten it and carry adverse effects. Supportive care and intranasal saline are both appropriate
  19. 12-year-old girl has had 2 weeks of dry cough and headache scattered crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial infiltrates Well appearing; eating normally T 38.0°C · oxygen saturation 97% on room air → Oral azithromycin → presumed Mycoplasma pneumonia in a well child is treated as an outpatient with a macrolide, or doxycycline (short courses are accepted under 8 years); it lacks a cell wall, so amoxicillin and intravenous ceftriaxone fail
  20. 3-year-old boy has had fever and a runny nose for 3 days and is irritable right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous no movement on pneumatic otoscopy External canal normal T 38.9°C · HR 128/min → Acute otitis media → a bulging, immobile, erythematous membrane is acute otitis media; mobility on pneumatic otoscopy is the discriminator. With fever and a bulging red membrane this is acute infection rather than effusion alone, and the normal canal leaves otitis externa out
  21. 64-year-old man who smokes has 2 days of high fever and confusion watery diarrhea crackles at the right base Returned from a cruise last week T 40.1°C · sodium 128 mEq/L → Legionella pneumophila → high fever, diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia in an older smoker after a cruise is Legionella: the urine antigen confirms. Mycoplasma is indolent in the young, and pneumococcus is the rigors and rusty sputum picture
  22. 3-year-old boy had a cold that was improving by day 5 on day 7, new fever nasal discharge worsening again, from both nostrils No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.8°C · HR 120/min · tympanic membranes mobile → Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → improvement, then new fever and worse discharge, is double worsening, the third door to acute bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate. The turn, not the day count or the color, crosses the door; allergy gives clear discharge with sneezing and itch
How NBME framed it: question 1

Previously healthy 10-year-old boy with 10 days of worsening cough a low-grade fever mild dyspnea on exertion diffuse crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: diffuse perihilar infiltrate

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Pneumonia due to respiratory syncytial virus: viral, with diffuse bilateral findings; but it causes wheezy lower respiratory disease in infants and children under 2, not at 10.
  • Congestive heart failure: a diffuse perihilar infiltrate with bilateral crackles also describes pulmonary edema; but in children it usually follows congenital heart disease, an arteriovenous fistula or severe malnutrition, and this child was previously healthy and febrile.
  • Tuberculosis: the cough is subacute; but there is no exposure, weight loss or night sweats, and the film shows no hilar adenopathy or cavitation.

Down to two: Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Streptococcus pneumoniae. Mycoplasma over pneumococcus: pneumococcus brings a productive cough, pleuritic chest pain and a single-lobe consolidation, not a gradual 10-day course with a diffuse film. A film that looks worse than the child is the Mycoplasma pattern. The stem never says atypical; age, onset and film carry the answer, and a macrolide treats it.

Common wrong answers Acute bacterial sinusitis for one-sided pus: purulence fits, but sinusitis is bilateral and usually febrile with cough; one-sided discharge in a playful, afebrile toddler is a foreign body. Allergic rhinitis because of a smoking father and a pet dog: risk factors, but allergy gives bilateral clear discharge with pale turbinates, not unilateral foul pus. Mucormycosis because of his human immunodeficiency virus infection: a CD4 count of 520/mm³ and red, swollen turbinates, not white or black, rule it out.
Pairs with Part I Hemolytic Anemia: the cold-agglutinin hemolysis Mycoplasma causes and the direct antiglobulin pattern that identifies it. Part I Tuberculosis: the child with a subacute cough and a known contact; is there weight loss, night sweats or hilar adenopathy?
Transferable rule

For each striking detail, ask what it adds to the diagnosis; a detail that only raises alarm is a distractor. When symptoms involve two compartments at once (upper and lower airway, as pharyngitis with an interstitial pneumonia in adults), ask which organisms span both: typical bacterial pneumonia does not cause pharyngitis.
